question: How does SOBER learn that a host's usage limit is spent, so its models are kept out of Jev's list and a run falls to the backup? Claude Code has no usage command (`claude --help`), Codex only a cached model list, OpenRouter's key usage sits behind opencode's key.

options.label: Probe each host before Jev
options.reason: Before `askJev`, run one tiny prompt per host the candidate list names (`claude -p` / `codex exec` / `opencode run`, `--model` of the cheapest entry) and read the exit: a limit or auth error drops that host's entries. Jev never sees a host that cannot run, which is exactly the ask. Result cached in `.sober/local/hosts.json` for a short TTL so a wave of dispatches probes once.
options.costLater: One real request per host per TTL — it spends a sliver of the very quota it checks, adds seconds to every dispatch, and the limit-error text per host is learned from captured output, so a host that rewords it goes unnoticed until a run fails anyway. A probe that passes at 99% still fails at 100% two minutes later.

options.label: Trust the start, fall to the backup on failure
options.reason: No probe. The primary runs; if the host exits before its first tool line with a limit or auth error, the run record marks `refused` and the backup starts in the same worktree. Zero extra requests, and the error text is read where it actually appears.
options.costLater: Jev still sees and can pick a host at 100% — the opposite of “should not see the Claude dispatcher at all”; the failed start shows in the record and the logs; and both picks can be on the same host, so a two-model fallback on one spent host fails twice.

options.label: Probe, and still fall to the backup
options.reason: The probe keeps a spent host out of Jev's list; the fallback catches what the probe missed (limit reached between probe and start, a provider down for one model). Each layer covers the other's hole.
options.costLater: Two mechanisms to test and to keep in step: the limit-text patterns live in one place per host adapter and both paths must use them. The cache TTL is a knob somebody has to pick (`dispatch.probeSeconds`); too long and a spent host is offered, too short and every dispatch pays a probe.
